first.rationale: Two funnel metrics are down (onboarding -4%, activation -6%), so the onboarding/activation path is the most direct lever on the current deficit, and memory_86 plus memory_31 both point that way. But the objective is sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue, and both of those memories are recorded only against proxy outcomes (completion rate, first-week activation, time-to-value) — neither states a revenue or retention result. That is exactly the gap the verification budget should close, so I pull memory_86's original record (the load-bearing one for the action I intend; memory_31 is the same family and partly redundant). The second pull goes to memory_73 rather than a memory I am not acting on, because promotional pricing is the loudest attractor in this situation (competitor entry pricing, price-sensitive SMB churn) and its claim of 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is the one most likely to be short-horizon: discount-acquired SMB cohorts routinely look good on acquisition and bad on retention and margin, which would actively damage the stated objective. If the archive shows memory_73 measured durable, post-discount revenue, promotional pricing becomes a live contender; if it measured a quarter of bookings, it is disqualified and I stop being pulled toward it. I deliberately did not spend a pull on memory_57 (referral) — it already carries a retention guardrail in its summary, and it is not responsive to a funnel decline — nor on memory_44, which I am not acting on directly. Key downstream risk I am carrying explicitly: memory_31's mechanism was 'cutting required fields at signup,' and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on the sales-assisted/demo path. Stripping qualification fields could raise activation counts while degrading lead quality and enterprise routing — a proxy win that is a qualified-revenue loss. So the experiment must be scoped to the SMB self-serve segment, leave the enterprise demo path untouched, and be judged on downstream qualified-pipeline and 30/90-day retention with a holdout, not on completion rate alone. Standard experiment with a holdout rather than broad rollout: the inherited evidence is 24-52 days old, was consolidated under different competitive conditions, and has not been validated against the revenue objective. If the memory_86 pull reveals the lift was completion-only with no retained-revenue follow-through, I downgrade to a small guarded test and reconsider activation_messaging (memory_91), which targets the larger 6% decline.

final.rationale: Both pulls paid off. exp_86 is the strongest available evidence for the objective: it is not a proxy-only result — completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3%, meaning the lift survived past the point where cohort quality usually shows. That is the one inherited belief now verified to move in the same direction as sustainable qualified revenue. exp_73 resolves the loudest attractor decisively against itself: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% are exactly the short-horizon numbers I suspected, and 30-day retention -12% with an explicit source conclusion not to generalize discounting. Promotional pricing is disqualified for this slot despite being the most emotionally responsive answer to the competitor's entry pricing — matching a discount war would buy a cohort that does not survive its first renewal and would damage the stated objective. Note the retention split is the whole decision: exp_86 +3% vs exp_73 -12%, same metric, opposite sign. So: simplify_onboarding, standard experiment with a holdout. Onboarding completion is the smaller declining metric (-4% vs activation's -6%), and I am choosing it over activation_messaging (memory_91) anyway because memory_91 remains unverified and its recorded outcomes are purely proxy — week-one engagement and first meaningful action — with no retention or revenue reading. Verified retention-positive evidence beats a larger unverified target. Onboarding also sits upstream of activation, so a completion lift should partially propagate into the activation number. Carrying forward the risk I flagged before, unresolved by these pulls: memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on the sales-assisted demo path. I spent no budget on either, so both remain unverified. Therefore the experiment is scoped to SMB self-serve only, leaves the enterprise demo path completely untouched, and does not remove qualification fields that feed lead routing — I shorten and resequence the flow rather than strip qualification data. exp_86 validated a shortened flow, not field removal; I am deliberately not treating those as the same intervention. Success criteria are downstream, not completion rate: qualified pipeline and 30/90-day retention against a holdout, with completion and time-to-value as leading indicators only. Residual uncertainty I am not pretending away: exp_86 is 24 days old and predates the competitor's entry pricing, so a funnel fix may not fully offset price-driven SMB losses even if it replicates. If the holdout shows completion up but retention flat or qualified pipeline down, that is a proxy win and a real loss, and I kill it rather than roll out. The competitive pricing pressure is a real problem that this experiment does not solve; the correct next move there is a durable packaging or value response evaluated on post-renewal revenue, not a discount, and it should get its own slot rather than being smuggled into this one.
